programs.haiku:
"""layers.0.mlp.down_proj:2305 -- a "grammar-terminology" detector (negative direction).

The component writes a negative value when the current token is a word naming a
grammatical or linguistic category (verb, clause, conditional, pronoun, plural, tense,
sentence, phrase, comma, passive, ...), or the word "speaker", or a Chinese/Japanese
grammar word (句 sentence, 词/詞 word, 语/語 language, 状 state, 态/態 voice). The
strength of the response is graded: category names such as "verb" or "clause" give
about -1, "sentence", "phrase", "passive" and "speaker" about -0.7, and looser
grammar-flavoured words such as "structure", "subject", "particle", "past", "present"
about -0.25. Every other token gives 0. The prediction depends only on the current
token, so the program keeps no state between positions.
"""

READS = ()

STRONG = set("""verb verbs verbal noun nouns pron pronoun pronouns oun ouns adjective adjectives adj
adverb adverbs conjunction conjunctions preposition participle clause clauses conditional tense
plural predicate predicates modal modals subjunctive indicative imperative""".split())
MEDIUM = set("""sentence sentences phrase phrases comma commas passive speaker speakers grammar
gramm lexical implication modifier modifiers mood""".split())
WEAK = set("""structure structures construction constructions statement statements subject subjects
particle particles syntax implies implied past present future perfect aspect voice article articles
singular suffix semantic""".split())
CJK_GRAMMAR = set("句詞词語语状態态")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if word in STRONG or token in CJK_GRAMMAR:
        value = -1.0
    elif word in MEDIUM:
        value = -0.7
    elif word in WEAK:
        value = -0.25
    else:
        value = 0.0
    return carry, value

programs.sol:
"""Approximate a grammatical coordination response and a rare NUL response.

Lowercase 'and' and 'or' are negative after adjectives and predicates.
Numbers, closing brackets, and longer comma-delimited clauses shift them
positive. NUL separators are positive after letters and near zero after spaces.
Other tokens default to zero: their lexical variation is not explained.
"""

READS = ()

ADJECTIVES = frozenset("""
able absolute abstract adjacent advanced american appropriate average
basic big black blue born bottom certain clean clear close cold common
complete complex constant content correct current daily dark dead deep
detailed different difficult direct double dry due easy efficient empty
entire equal european excellent existing extra far fast few final fine
first fluid foreign former free fresh front full fun given good grand
great green growing half happy hard healthy heavy high hot human ill
important independent inner interesting key kind known large last late
leading left legal light likely limited little living local long low lower
main major male many maximum mean minimum missing mixed mobile modern more
most multiple near net new next nice old online open other outer overall
own particular past patient perfect popular prepared present pretty
private proper random raw ready real recent red regular related relevant
required rich right round safe second secret separate short signed
significant similar simple single small soft solid standard straight
strong super sure third top total true unique united unknown upper valid
western white whole wide written wrong young
""".split())

FUNCTION_WORDS = frozenset("""
about after all any as at before between both by during each either every
few for from he her him his i in into it its less many me more most much
my near of on one only our outside over she since some such that their
them these they this those through to two under until us we what which who
with without you your
""".split())

VERBS = frozenset("""
achieve am are ask be become been bring build call came change come create
develop did do does done feel find found get give given go got had has
have help include is keep kept know known learn leave left let live look
made make move need perform play provide put read return run said say see
seem seen set show spoken take taken tell think thought try use want was
went were work write written
""".split())

def adjective(word):
    if word in ADJECTIVES:
        return True
    if len(word) > 5 and word.endswith(
        ('ous', 'ful', 'less', 'ive', 'ical', 'able', 'ible', 'al', 'ic',
         'ary', 'ish')
    ):
        return True
    for ending in ('er', 'est'):
        if word.endswith(ending):
            base = word[:-len(ending)]
            return base in ADJECTIVES or base + 'e' in ADJECTIVES
    return False


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        carry = (doc, '', '', 0, 0, 0, '')
    _, previous, last_word, count, gap, position, tail = carry
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    value = 0.0
    if token == '\0':
        value = 0.001 if previous.isspace() else 0.014
        if previous.isalpha():
            value = 0.063
        if position < 5 and not previous.isspace():
            value += 0.023
    elif token in (' and', ' or'):
        is_and = token == ' and'
        p, word = previous.strip(), last_word.lower()
        if ',' in p:
            value = (-0.004 + 0.119 * min(gap, 15) / 15 if is_and
                     else -0.021 + 0.065 * min(gap, 15) / 15)
        elif any(c in p for c in ')]}'):
            value = 0.066 if is_and else 0.102
        elif p and p[-1].isdigit():
            value = 0.020 if is_and else 0.052
        elif p and not p[-1].isalpha():
            value = 0.012 if is_and else 0.038
        else:
            value = -0.048 if is_and else 0.010
            if adjective(word):
                value -= 0.120 if is_and else 0.092
            if word in FUNCTION_WORDS:
                value -= 0.053 if is_and else 0.065
            if (word in VERBS or
                    (len(word) > 4 and word.endswith(('ed', 'ing', 'ly')))):
                value -= 0.061 if is_and else 0.058

    # Join split words, counting word starts between punctuation marks.
    for char in token:
        if char.isalpha():
            if not tail:
                count += 1
            tail = (tail + char)[-40:]
            last_word = tail
        else:
            tail = ''
            if char in ',;:.!?\n':
                gap, count = count, 0
    return (doc, token, last_word, count, gap, position + 1, tail), float(value)
programs.haiku:
"""Component layers.0.mlp.down_proj:2306, read as a conjunction "and" detector.

What it responds to, from its activations on training text:
  * English " and", the main driver. The sign depends on the word just before it:
    - after an adjective (or a word ending like one: "simple and easy",
      "quiet, thoughtful and intelligent"): strongly negative;
    - after any other word: mildly negative;
    - after a comma or closing bracket (joining clauses or items): mildly positive.
  * The null byte (token "\\x00") that UTF-16 text puts after each ASCII letter:
    mildly positive, unless it follows a space.
Everything else has no simple concept behind it (its activation is a diffuse,
token-specific signal), so the program predicts 0 there.
"""

READS = ()

ADJECTIVE_ENDINGS = ("ful", "ous", "ive", "al", "ic", "ble", "ed", "ing", "ent", "ant", "less", "able")

# Mean activation per context, fitted on training text
AFTER_ADJECTIVE = -0.11
AFTER_WORD = -0.06
AFTER_PUNCTUATION = 0.035
NULL_AFTER_LETTER = 0.07


def is_word(text):
    return text.isalpha() and text.isascii()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    before = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip() if len(prefix.token_strings) > 1 else ""
    if token == " and":
        if is_word(before) and before.lower().endswith(ADJECTIVE_ENDINGS):
            return carry, AFTER_ADJECTIVE
        if is_word(before):
            return carry, AFTER_WORD
        return carry, AFTER_PUNCTUATION
    if token == "\x00" and is_word(before):
        return carry, NULL_AFTER_LETTER
    return carry, 0.0

def step(carry, prefix, upstream):

    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    previous = prefix.token_strings[-2] if n > 1 else ''
    same_doc = n > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-1] == prefix.document_ids[-2]

    if token == '\x00' and same_doc:
        if previous and all(c.isascii() and c.isalnum() for c in previous):
            return None, 0.07
        if previous == ' ':
            return None, -0.01
        if previous:
            return None, 0.02
    if (previous == '\x00' and same_doc and token
            and all(c.isascii() and c.isalnum() for c in token)):
        return None, 0.02
    return None, 0.0

programs.haiku:
"""Layer-0 MLP output component 2307: a negative "m-piece inside a word" detector.

What it does: it goes negative on a short token that starts with the letter m (or a
look-alike m in another script: Greek mu, Cyrillic em, Arabic meem, Thai mo, the
ma/mi/mu/me/mo kana, Hangul syllables starting with M) when that token continues the
word begun by the previous token, with no space in between, as in "Dhan|mon|di",
"Chris Cle|mons", "Till|man". Longer m-pieces get a smaller negative value, and an m
after a space, a digit or punctuation (or a capital M in a short piece) gets little or
nothing. Every other token predicts 0.
"""

import unicodedata

READS = ()

# Multipliers for the strength of the response: short (<= 3 characters) m-pieces that
# continue a word are strongest; capital M and other scripts are weaker.
SHORT_LIMIT = 3


def _m_script(ch):
    """Which m-like letter `ch` is: "m" (Latin lowercase), "M" (Latin capital), "other"
    (Greek mu, Cyrillic em, Arabic meem, Thai mo, kana ma-row, Hangul M-syllables), or None."""
    if ch == "m":
        return "m"
    if ch == "M":
        return "M"
    try:
        name = unicodedata.name(ch)
    except ValueError:
        return None
    if (
        name in ("GREEK SMALL LETTER MU", "ARABIC LETTER MEEM", "THAI CHARACTER MO MA")
        or name.startswith(("CYRILLIC SMALL LETTER EM", "CYRILLIC CAPITAL LETTER EM"))
        or name.startswith(("KATAKANA LETTER M", "HIRAGANA LETTER M", "HANGUL SYLLABLE M"))
    ):
        return "other"
    return None


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if not token or token[0] == " ":
        return carry, 0.0
    kind = _m_script(token[0])
    if kind is None:
        return carry, 0.0
    # The previous token counts only within the same document.
    same_doc = len(prefix) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
    previous = prefix.token_strings[-2] if same_doc else ""
    continues_word = bool(previous) and previous[-1:].isalpha()
    short = len(token) <= SHORT_LIMIT
    if not continues_word:
        return carry, -0.15 if (kind == "m" and short) else 0.0
    strength = {"m": 1.2, "M": 1.0, "other": 0.55}[kind]
    if not short:
        strength *= 0.4
    return carry, -strength

programs.sol:
"""Recognize unspaced word starts following a separately tokenized separator.

The main response is negative at Latin word pieces after a lone hyphen,
slash, underscore, dot, or opening parenthesis. Merged punctuation has a
much weaker response. Single ASCII letters and non-Latin scripts are weaker
than multi-letter Latin pieces. Newlines and document starts are not triggers.
"""
import unicodedata

READS = ()

# Separators have different response strengths; these are activation units.
SEPARATORS = {
    '-': 1.39, '/': 1.36, '_': 1.63, '.': 1.27,
    '(': 1.15, '\t': 1.09, ' ': 0.96,
    ':': 0.87, ',': 0.77, '=': 0.69,
    '[': 0.48, '<': 0.48,
    '+': 0.30, '*': 0.28, "'": 0.27,
    '>': 0.23, '?': 0.23, '&': 0.20,
    ')': 0.18, ';': 0.17, '\xa0': 0.15,
    '#': 0.15, '\\': 0.12, '"': 0.11, '|': 0.07,
}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    previous = carry[1] if carry is not None and carry[0] == doc else ''
    value = 0.0
    if token and token[0].isalpha() and previous:
        script = unicodedata.name(token[0], '')
        if 'LATIN' in script:
            weight = 1.0
            if len(token) == 1:
                weight = (0.22 if token.isupper() else 0.10)
                if not token.isascii():
                    weight = 0.60
        elif 'CYRILLIC' in script:
            weight = 0.30
        elif 'GREEK' in script:
            weight = 0.28
        else:
            weight = 0.0
        strength = SEPARATORS.get(previous, 0.0)
        if not strength and len(previous) > 1:
            tail = previous[-1]
            if tail in '/(,=\'':
                strength = 0.12
            elif tail in '-_:[<':
                strength = 0.04
        value = -weight * strength
    return (doc, token), float(value)
programs.haiku:
"""layers.0.mlp.down_proj:2308 -- a "glued word after a joiner" detector.

What it does: this component goes clearly negative on a plain Latin-letter word that
is attached, with no space, to the character just before it when that character is a
joiner in code, paths, URLs or compound names: the second half of `prettier-plugin-astro`,
`src/commands`, `non-UTF-8`, `node_modules/figures`, `my_var`. The strongest joiners are
underscore, hyphen, slash and dot (about -1.3 to -1.5); opening bracket, colon, comma and
equals are weaker (about -0.5 to -0.9); `<`, quote and `)` are weaker still. Digits
after a joiner (dates, fractions), words after a space, and CJK text give about zero.
A hyphen followed by a space ("a- b") gives a small positive value.

The program predicts this directly: a value per joiner, zero everywhere else. It has no
state beyond the previous token.
"""

import re

READS = ()

# Typical activation of a glued Latin word after each joiner token (from training rows).
JOINER_VALUE = {
    "_": -1.5,
    "-": -1.4,
    "/": -1.35,
    ".": -1.3,
    "\t": -1.0,
    "(": -0.9,
    ":": -0.9,
    ",": -0.8,
    "=": -0.7,
    "[": -0.5,
    "<": -0.4,
    "'": -0.25,
    " /": -0.25,
    ">": -0.2,
    ")": -0.2,
}
HYPHEN_THEN_SPACE = 0.2  # small positive value on the space after a hyphen


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # Position 0 of a document has no previous token in the same document.
    if prefix.position == 0 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]:
        return None, 0.0
    cur = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2]
    if prev == "-" and cur[:1] == " ":
        return None, HYPHEN_THEN_SPACE
    if re.fullmatch(r"[A-Za-z]+", cur) and prev in JOINER_VALUE:
        return None, JOINER_VALUE[prev]
    return None, 0.0

"""Component layers.0.mlp.down_proj:2324: the "hard g" fragment detector.

What it does, in plain terms:
  * It fires on the letter g (or G, or the Cyrillic г) when that letter is a piece
    *inside* a word: a word fragment that is glued onto the piece before it, such as
    "gen" in "ge|neric", "gr" in "...gr", "GB" or "gu" in a longer word. Activation
    is positive, about +0.6.
  * It is strongly negative (about -0.9) on a standalone capital G that starts a
    word or sits after punctuation: " G", "(G", ".G", "G" at the start of a line.
    That is the G of "G-protein", "Group G", "George", and similar.
  * Everything else (including g inside whole words like " using", "ing", and g at
    the start of a spaced word such as " get") is about 0.

The sign flips with word position, not with the letter alone: the same "G" is
negative at a word start and near 0 when glued to a preceding word piece.
"""

READS = ()

G_LETTERS = "gGгГ"             # Latin g/G and Cyrillic г/Г, the /g/ letters
PUNCT = "(.-/\"'[`"             # characters that open a new word in code or prose
GLUED_POS = 0.6                  # g fragment continuing a word
STANDALONE_G = -0.9              # capital G starting a word
GLUED_G = -0.2                   # capital G glued to the piece before it


def _ends_word_piece(text: str) -> bool:
    return bool(text) and text[-1].isalnum()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    core = tok.lstrip(" " + PUNCT)
    if not core or core[0] not in G_LETTERS:
        return None, 0.0
    # Is the previous token a piece of the same word (same document)?
    glued = False
    if len(prefix.token_strings) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]:
        glued = not tok[:1].isspace() and tok[:1] not in PUNCT and _ends_word_piece(
            prefix.token_strings[-2]
        )
    if core == "G" or core == "Г":
        return None, (GLUED_G if glued else STANDALONE_G)
    return None, (GLUED_POS if glued else 0.0)

This component is almost entirely a lexical detector. It fires (about 0.5 to 1.0)
on a few families of tokens and is near zero elsewhere:

- "every" / "Every" / "EVERY" (strongest common word)
- "null" / "NULL" / "nil"-style code words (null, NULL, Null, /null, (null)

- "schedule", "scheduled", "scheduling", "scheduler" (about 0.85)
- "attribute", "attributes", "attr", "attrs", "setAttribute", "hasattr" (about 0.75)
- "drop", "dropped", "dropping", "crop" (about 0.5)
- the second half of the abbreviations "e.g." and "i.e." (the ".g" after "e",
  the ".e" after "i"), about 0.75 and 0.7; "U.S." gives a weaker 0.3

Everything not in these families predicts 0.

EVERY = 0.8
NULL = 0.65
KNOWLEDGE = 0.7
SCHEDULE = 0.85
ATTRIBUTE = 0.75
DROP = 0.5
E_G = 0.75
I_E = 0.7
U_S = 0.3

    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    before = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip() if prefix.position > 0 else ""

    elif word == ".e" and before == "i":

token is the C++/Rust/PHP scope operator "::" (as in `std::string`, `Foo::new`,

a number, as in "2024-04-12", "3-2", "555-1234", "3+2", "28/10", "10-year", "p. 180-181",
"0.014*298", "3×4". These are the joiners between two numbers: ranges, dates, phone
numbers, sums, products. The strongest case is a bare hyphen or en dash right after a digit

READS = ()

DIGITS = set("0123456789０１２３４５６７８９")
DASHES = "-–−－"

AFTER_DIGIT = {
    "-": 4.7, "－": 4.7, "–": 4.6, "—": 3.0, "−": 2.5,
    " -": 1.2, " –": 2.1, " −": 1.4,
    "+": 2.0, " +": 1.2,
    "/": 1.0, "*": 0.7, "×": 0.7, "^": 1.1,
    " to": 1.1, " and": 0.4,

"""Component layers.0.mlp.down_proj:2331: a "word-piece inside a non-English word" detector.

What it does, in plain terms:
- The tokenizer often splits one word into several tokens. This component fires on a
  later piece of such a word: a token with no leading space, made only of lower-case
  letters (e.g. "lag" in "Verlag", "рос" in "спрос", "gang" in "Sonnenaufgang").
- Capitalised pieces, pieces with punctuation or digits, and CJK characters give 0.
- How strongly it fires depends on the script and the language of the recent text.
  Cyrillic, Arabic, Hangul and Greek pieces are strong; Latin-script pieces are weak in
  English passages (about 0.05) and strong in German passages (about 0.5), and ordinary
  Latin pieces in other languages sit in between (about 0.2).
- A piece right after another word-piece (the word is still being built) is boosted 1.3x.
- Russian inflectional endings (-ой, -ых, -ский ...) are not word stems, so they get 0.

Why: the program is a readable rule set, not a token table. It needs only the current token,
the previous token and about 60 tokens of recent text in the same document, so it runs
causally, one position at a time.
"""
import unicodedata

READS = ()

ENGLISH = set("the and of to is in that for it with as was on be by this are".split())
GERMAN = set("der die und ist nicht das den dem ein eine zu mit auf für von sich auch im des es".split())
SCRIPT_WEIGHT = {"CYRILLIC": 0.37, "ARABIC": 0.54, "HANGUL": 0.33, "GREEK": 0.16,
                 "THAI": 0.18, "HIRAGANA": 0.08, "CJK": 0.0, "KATAKANA": 0.0, "LATIN": 0.2}
RU_ENDINGS = set("ой ый ая ые ого ной ных ский ская ское ов ие ии ы и е а я о у ю ым им ую ом ам ах ями".split())


def script_of(text):
    """The script of the first letter in a token, by its Unicode name."""
    for ch in text:
        if ch.isalpha():
            name = unicodedata.name(ch, "")
            for key in SCRIPT_WEIGHT:
                if key in name:
                    return key
            return "LATIN" if ord(ch) <= 0x024F else "OTHER"
    return "NONE"


def is_fragment(s):
    """A later piece of a word: letters only, glued to the previous token, not capitalised."""
    return bool(s) and s[0] != " " and s.isalpha() and "�" not in s and not s[0].isupper()

    t = prefix.position
    docs = prefix.document_ids
    # Recent text of the same document (at most 60 tokens back), lower-cased words.
    start = t
    while start > 0 and start > t - 60 and docs[start - 1] == docs[t]:
        start -= 1
    recent = "".join(prefix.token_strings[start:t]).lower()
    words, cur = set(), ""
    for ch in recent:
        if ch.isalpha():
            cur += ch
        elif cur:
            words.add(cur)
            cur = ""
    en = len(words & ENGLISH)
    de = len(words & GERMAN)

    s = prefix.token_strings[t]
    if not is_fragment(s):
        return carry, 0.0
    sc = script_of(s)
    w = SCRIPT_WEIGHT.get(sc, 0.1)
    if sc == "LATIN":
        if en >= 2 and en > 2 * de:
            w = 0.05
        elif de >= 2 and de > 2 * en:
            w = 0.5
    if sc == "CYRILLIC" and s in RU_ENDINGS:
        w = 0.0
    prev = prefix.token_strings[t - 1] if t > 0 and docs[t - 1] == docs[t] else ""
    if is_fragment(prev):
        w *= 1.3
    return carry, float(w)

it follows a backslash, even if joined to the next word. Extra backslashes
weaken this response. Newline/tab escapes merged into one token are weaker;
adjacent escaped whitespace strengthens them. Isolated backslash-t can be

smaller responses, as do chat tags and escape-introducing punctuation.
Ordinary text is predicted near zero.

    '<|im_end|>': 1.82,
    '<|im_start|>': -0.01,
    '<tool_call>': -0.075,
    '</tool_call>': 0.064,
    '<tool_response>': -0.075,
    '</tool_response>': -0.13,
    '<think>': 0.134,
    '</think>': 0.066,

        elif token == 't':

"""Backslash escape letters and end-of-turn tokens (layer 0, MLP down_proj, component 2332).

This component is silent on almost all text. It fires on two kinds of token:

1. Text written as backslash escape codes, the way code, JSON, regexes and
   logs spell a newline or tab. The letter after a backslash is strong for
   "n" (the n of \\n, about 1.2) and moderate for "x" (\\x41, about 0.5). The
   escape written as one token, "\\t" (about 0.5) and "\\n" (about 0.3), also fires.
2. The end-of-turn token <|im_end|>, which closes every chat message (about 1.8).

Everything else is predicted as 0. Other letters after a backslash, such as
\\t's "t" or LaTeX commands like \\alpha, stay near 0.

The program is stateless: it only looks at the current token and the one before
it, and does not look across document boundaries.
"""

ESCAPE_N = 1.23       # "n" right after a backslash, as in \n
ESCAPE_X = 0.46       # "x" right after a backslash, as in \x41
TAB_TOKEN = 0.50      # the single token that is a backslash followed by t
NEWLINE_TOKEN = 0.27  # the single token that is a backslash followed by n


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if token == "<|im_end|>":
        return carry, END_OF_TURN
    if token == "\\t":
        return carry, TAB_TOKEN
    if token == "\\n":
        return carry, NEWLINE_TOKEN
    same_doc = len(prefix) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if same_doc and prefix.token_strings[-2].endswith("\\"):

        if token.startswith("x"):
            return carry, ESCAPE_X

the current token starts with a Thai consonant or a Thai leading vowel (เ แ โ ใ ไ), i.e.
the first letter of a new Thai syllable. Thai is written without spaces between words, so
these letters mark where syllables (and often words) begin. Tokens that begin with a Thai

byte fragments, other special tokens) is 0.

WEAK_ONSET_VALUE = -2.2
LEADING_VALUE = -3.1
SIGN_VALUE = -0.8
END_OF_TURN_VALUE = -0.5

    """The first Thai character in a token's text, or '' if it has none."""
    for ch in text:

    return ""

    text = prefix.token_strings[-1]

        value = LEADING_VALUE
    elif ch in VOWEL_SIGNS_AND_TONES:
        value = SIGN_VALUE

    return carry, value

"""Legal-drafting register: layer 0 MLP component 2341 (a negative, context-scaled response).

What it does. The component is pushed strongly negative by the vocabulary of contracts and
legal drafting, and most of all by the modal "shall" (and "SHALL"). Other strong triggers are
defined-term nouns of agreements ("Agreement", "Agent", "Affiliate", "Borrower", "Guarantor",
"Participant", "Licensee", "hereby", "herein"), the legal quantifiers "any", "such", "under",
"other", and "or" when it links such terms. Ordinary function words (of, to, the, and) barely
move it.

Shouted (ALL-CAPS) legal words get a weaker version of the same response. Other words are ~0.

Why the strength depends on context. The response grows with how much legal language came
earlier in the same document, measured by a decaying running count (decay 0.98 per token,
reset at each new document; capped at 3). So "or" or "any" is near zero in chat or prose and
strongly negative inside a loan agreement.

The weights were fitted by least squares on 2048 training rows, one (base, gain) pair per
word group, then rounded. On held-out eval rows it explains 17% of the activation variance
(r = 0.42), and putting its predictions in the model gives 64% of the KL change that
switching the component off causes.
"""

SHALL = {"shall"}
STRONG = {
    "agreement", "agent", "affiliate", "borrow", "guar", "agre", "ement", "loyee",
    "hereby", "herein", "otherwise",
}  # word pieces like "Borrow|er", "Guar|antor", "AGRE|EMENT" included
DEFINED = {
    "borrower", "borrowers", "guarantor", "lender", "participant", "licensee", "licensor",
    "party", "parties", "company", "section", "license", "collateral", "loan", "plan",
    "hereof", "hereunder", "thereof", "applicable", "pursuant", "foregoing", "subsection",
    "clause", "notice", "deemed", "subparagraph", "employee", "substantially", "respect",
    "rights", "agreed",
}
QUANTIFIERS = {"any", "such", "under", "other"}
WEAK = {"be": 0.22, "not": 0.22, "may": 0.22, "all": 0.22, "or": 0.37, "of": 0.10, "to": 0.08,
        "and": 0.08, "the": 0.06}
DECAY = 0.98
READS = ()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    density, doc = carry if carry is not None else (0.0, None)
    if prefix.document_ids[-1] != doc:
        density = 0.0
    raw = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip()
    word = raw.lower()
    gain = min(density, 3.0)

        value = -(1.2 + 0.45 * gain)
    elif word in STRONG:
        value = -(0.2 + 0.6 * gain)
    elif word in DEFINED:
        value = -(0.15 + 0.35 * gain)
    elif word in QUANTIFIERS:
        value = -(0.1 + 0.43 * gain)
    elif word in WEAK:
        value = -WEAK[word] * gain
    elif raw.isupper() and len(raw) > 1:
        value = -0.13 * gain  # shouted legal words, e.g. "AGREEMENT", "LOYEE" pieces
    else:
        value = 0.0

in a 64-token window weaken short ung forms; preceding token length and case
also modulate them. Longer containing words receive a decaying response.

spelling/context approximation, not a token-ID lookup or a model simulation.

mit von zu für nicht ist werden wird auf im am sich auch als bei aus nach oder'''.split())
ENGLISH = frozenset('''the and of to a is for that with on by from was are it
this be at'''.split())

GERMAN_SUFFIX_FRAGMENTS = {'nung', 'zung', 'bung', 'igung'}
IRREGULAR_PAST = {'hung', 'sung', 'swung'}


def response(raw, german, english, previous):
    word = raw.strip()
    text = word.lower()
    if '&&' in text:
        return -1.12
    if '||' in text:
        return -0.25
    if text == 'und':
        return -0.43
    if text in UNG_FORMS:
        value = -5.20 + 1.83 * (1.0 - exp(-german / 4.0))
        value -= 0.58 * (1.0 - exp(-english / 4.0))
        value += 0.31 * min(8, len(previous))
        value -= 0.96 * previous.istitle()
        value += 0.71 * raw.startswith(' ')
        value -= 0.28 * word.isupper()
        value += 0.65 * word.istitle()
        return max(-7.0, min(-1.0, value)) * UNG_FORMS[text]
    if 'ung' in text and 'oung' not in text:
        if text in IRREGULAR_PAST and word.islower() and raw.startswith(' '):

        left, right = text.split('ung', 1)

        value = -3.0 * exp(-0.30 * max(0, len(left)-1) - 0.35 * len(right))
        if left and right:  # Medial ung is weaker than an exposed ending.
            value *= 0.60
        if len(left) > 2:
            value *= 0.83

        return -2.4 if text == '肺' else -1.5

        return -0.6
    if text.startswith(('chunk', 'thunk', 'lunch', 'punch', 'dunk', 'launch')):
        return -0.75
    if text in {'unc', 'unk', 'unch', 'unft', 'unction'}:
        return -0.75
    if text in {'ng', 'ug', 'ings'}:
        return -0.22
    return 0.0

    document = prefix.document_ids[-1]

    raw = prefix.token_strings[-1]

    english += flags[1]

        english -= recent[0][1]

"""Sentence endings, strongest near the beginning of the visible document.

A period combined with a line break has a large negative response which fades
as more tokens of the document are visible. It is stronger on the first line
and when the current line makes up much of the visible text. Longer decoded
token pieces increase this response. The curves distinguish paragraph breaks
and closing punctuation. Bare periods and question/exclamation line endings
use smaller curves; standalone line breaks have a positive early pulse.
A space before a period halves that response. Ordinary text is zero.
The smooth curves below were fitted on training text, not on token IDs.
"""

READS = ()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        position, line_chars, chars, first_line = 0, 0, 0, True
    else:
        _, position, line_chars, chars, first_line = carry
        position += 1
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    line_fraction = line_chars / (chars + 20)
    next_line_chars = (len(token.rsplit("\n", 1)[-1])
                       if "\n" in token else line_chars + len(token))
    carry = (doc, position, next_line_chars, chars + len(token),
             first_line and "\n" not in token)
    body = token.rstrip('\r\n')
    newlines = token.count('\n')
    value = 0.0

    if newlines and body and body.count('.') + body.count('。') == 1:
        # Only sentence punctuation, not dots embedded in words or ellipses.
        if all(c in ' .。()[]{}\'"“”’»`%\t' for c in body):
            blank = newlines >= 2
            if '。' in body:
                value = 0.10 - 2.72 / (1 + position / 23) ** 1.58
                value -= 0.04 * line_fraction + 0.19 * first_line
            else:
                decay = (1 + position / 17.7) ** -1.25
                average_piece_chars = min(10.0, chars / (position + 1))
                amplitude = 2.22 - 0.38 * blank + 0.24 * average_piece_chars
                baseline = 0.059 + 0.059 * blank
                value = baseline - amplitude * decay
                value -= 0.169 * line_fraction + 0.244 * first_line
                if body.endswith('.') and len(body.strip()) > 1:
                    value -= 0.18 if not blank else 0.075
                    value += 0.35 * decay
                elif body[-1] in '\'"“”’»':
                    value = 0.05 - 2.33 / (1 + position / 16) ** 1.25
                    value -= 0.18 * first_line
            if position == 0:
                value = -1.83 if blank else -2.34
            if body.startswith(" ") and body.strip() == ".":
                value *= 0.5
    elif newlines and body.strip() in ('!', '?', '！', '？'):
        value = (0.14 if '!' in body or '！' in body else 0.05)
        value -= 0.8 / (1 + position / 70) ** 3.3

        value = 0.02 - 0.5 / (1 + position / 60) ** 5
        if position == 0:
            value = -0.21
    elif not body and newlines:
        if newlines >= 2:
            value = -0.038 + 1.07 / (1 + position / 2) ** 0.94
        else:
            value = 0.004 + 0.75 / (1 + position / 2.4) ** 5

    return carry, float(value)

"""Sentence-end line breaks near the start of a document.

Component layers.0.mlp.down_proj:2349 goes strongly negative on a sentence-ending
punctuation mark that is immediately followed by a line break (".\\n", ".\\n\\n",
"。\\n", ".”\\n"), and only when that break comes early in its document. The first
such break in a document is the strongest; the effect fades over roughly the first
100 tokens and is gone after a few hundred. A bare sentence-final "." (no newline)
gives a much weaker version of the same signal. Everything else is about zero.

(the model resets position at each document boundary), and scales the response by
exp(-tokens_since_start / TAU).

LINE_BREAK_GAIN = -2.1   # sentence end + line break, at the document start
BARE_PERIOD_GAIN = -0.18  # sentence end with no line break
SENTENCE_END = ".!?。”\""


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # carry = (document id of previous token, tokens since its start)
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        pos = 0
    else:
        pos = carry[1] + 1
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    decay = math.exp(-pos / TAU)

    return (doc, pos), float(value)

  It is quiet on most tokens. Its large activations sit on word *fragments*: a word that the

  piece's vowels: pieces with a, e or i (an, ar, ah, ern, ra, in) tend to be positive, and
  pieces with o or u (oud, ote, ut, ob, oz) tend to be negative.

a/e/i and no o/u, -0.005 for one with o/u and no a/e/i, and 0 everywhere else. It only reads

table (about 20k token strings) reaches about 12% held out, but that is a lexicon with no
concept behind it, so it is not used here.

MAX_LEN = 5
MIN_LEN = 2

NEG_VALUE = -0.005  # fragments with o or u (and no a, e or i)

    """True if the newest token is letters only, no leading space, and not a document's first token."""
    if prefix.position == 0 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]:

        return carry, POS_VALUE
    if has_ou and not has_aei:

    return carry, 0.0

    word = token.strip()

What it does: this component goes strongly negative on a verb of possession or
obligation -- "have", "get", "give", "obtain", "need", "had" -- when it directly
follows a person subject, above all "we" ("we have" ~ -3, "we get" ~ -3.4),
then "you" (~ -2), "I" (~ -1.5), and only weakly after modals/"to" ("to have"
~ -0.9, "will have" ~ -1). It is near zero for other verbs (do, make, take, use,
be) and for the same verbs after third-person nouns ("engines have" ~ 0).
A smaller negative response goes to "side"/"sides" (as in "both sides", "left side").

subject weight, with the sign flipped so the output is negative. Everything
else predicts 0.

    " have": 3.0, " Have": 3.0, "'ve": 3.0, "’ve": 3.0,
    " get": 3.0, " getting": 3.0, " got": 3.0,
    " give": 3.0, " gives": 3.0, " giving": 3.0, " gave": 3.0,
    " obtain": 3.0, " obtained": 3.0, " obtaining": 3.0, " reach": 3.0,
    " need": 2.0, " had": 2.0,
    " side": 1.0, " sides": 1.0,

    " we": 1.0, " We": 1.0,
    " you": 0.6, " You": 0.6,
    " I": 0.5,
    " to": 0.3, " will": 0.3, " would": 0.3, " must": 0.3,
    " should": 0.3, " can": 0.3, " might": 0.3,
}

def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    tokens = prefix.token_strings

"""layers.0.mlp.down_proj:2365, read as a rule on the current token's text.

This component reacts to the punctuation and line breaks that end a line, and it
ignores almost everything else:

* Three or more line breaks in a row (":\\n\\n\\n", ")\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n", "\\n\\n\\n") give a
  large positive value, about +2.5. These are the component's strongest responses.
* A question mark fused with other punctuation (",", ".", ":", ")") is strongly negative,
  about -2. A question mark ending a line or a quote ("?\\n\\n", '?"') is about -1.
  A bare "?" token on its own is inert, and so are code operators such as "!=".
* An exclamation mark fused with punctuation or a line break ("!\\n", "!(") is about -0.8.
* An opening bracket at the end of a line (" {\\n", "(\\n", "[\\n") is about +0.6.
* A blank line after closing code punctuation (";\\n\\n", ")\\n\\n", "}\\n\\n") is about +0.3,
  and so is a tab then a newline ("\\t\\n"). A bare "\\n\\n" token is about +0.2.
* Everything else, including ordinary words and single newlines, is 0.

Each rule is a rough class mean. The rule set predicts the sign and the rough size of
the activation; it doesn't reproduce the per-token detail or the small diffuse part.
"""

QUESTION = "?？"
EXCLAIM = "!！"
CODE_END = ";)}]>"


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    s = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    body = s.strip(" \t")  # the token without spaces or tabs
    newlines = body.count("\n")

        return None, -1.0  # ?\n, ?", ?\n\n : question mark ending a line or quote

        return None, -0.8

        return None, 0.6
    if newlines == 2 and end[-1:] in CODE_END:
        return None, 0.3
    if body == "\n\n":

    if s == "\t\n":
        return None, 0.3
    return None, 0.0
